description: We are Horizon 4, an interdisciplinary team of aerospace engineering students and developers from Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM). United by a passion for space exploration and systems engineering, our mission is to make complex space mission design intuitive, educational, and deeply engaging. By combining rigorous orbital mechanics with interactive software development, we built an immersive platform that bridges theoretical engineering concepts with real-world operational challenges.
summary: Build Your Rocket is a browser-based simulator driven by physics in aerospace engineering and collaborative mission control game built by the Horizon 4 Production Team. It is a platform that allows players to design, analyse and build their very own spacecraft for selected missions It can be played in either Solo or in a 4-player co-op gameplay.

System Architecture: Engineered as a responsive, client-side browser application utilizing high-performance canvas rendering and real-time numerical solvers. The core engine computes orbital mechanics, inverse-square solar attenuation, and dynamic mass-budget calculations instantaneously.

Engineering Trade-Offs & Coupled Solver: The platform operates on fundamental aerospace relationships, dynamically computing dry mass (mdry), propellant mass fraction, and Delta-V (V) trade-offs whenever critical components—such as Tantalum Radiation Vault Shields (110kg) or Ice-Penetrating SAR Radars (85kg)—are integrated.

Multiplayer Cooperative (Co-Op) Architecture: To replicate authentic aerospace project management, the platform features a 4-player room-code co-op mode distributing responsibilities across specialized roles:

  1. Commander: Directs mission charter, difficulty scaling, target orbit profiles, and holds final launch authority.
  2. Systems Lead: Optimizes power subsystems, avionics, thermal/radiation protection, and commands mitigation protocols during emergency anomalies (e.g., solar storms, cryo-valve failures).
  3. Science Investigator: Manages instrument payload integration and verifies minimum science return thresholds.

Flight Officer: Manages propulsion hardware, communication frequencies, and telemetry tracking during mission execution.

System Design and Operational Workflow

Introduction to the Space Mission Simulator Architecture

The space mission simulator is an interactive, multi-phase aerospace engineering and mission planning platform designed to evaluate interplanetary trajectory design, spacecraft subsystem sizing, launch vehicle integration, and real-time operational decision-making. The simulation bridges theoretical orbital mechanics (Tsiolkovsky rocket equation), spacecraft subsystems (power, propulsion, avionics, thermal/radiation protection), and real-time stochastic anomaly management.

Phase 1: Exploration Charter Selection

The mission lifecycle begins with the selection of a deep-space exploration charter. Each planetary target introduces severe astrophysical trade-offs governing Delta-V budgets, solar power attenuation, communication latencies, and environmental hazards:

  • Lunar Exploration: Focuses on permanently shadowed polar craters or equatorial survey targets, featuring high solar flux and minimal light delay.
  • Mars Astrobiology: Tasks the spacecraft with analyzing ancient lacustrine sediments, subsurface permafrost, or atmospheric signatures. Governed by moderate solar flux and short-to-medium communication light delays.
  • Outer Planet / Ocean Worlds: Navigates intense radiation belts and extreme solar attenuation to study outer planet moons and cryovolcanic activity, demanding robust RTG power sources and extended communication latencies.

Phase 2: Spacecraft Blueprint and Subsystem Assembly

Once a destination is chosen, engineers utilize the Blueprint Bay to assemble the spacecraft bus within mass and financial constraints (e.g., adhering to strict payload fairing capacity limits).

  • Hardware Catalog & Subsystem Integration: Components are categorized into Launchers, Chassis/Buses (such as modular CubeSats, Deep Space Hex-Buses, and Flagship Platform Busses), Power Subsystems (e.g., Solar arrays, Li-Ion battery banks, and Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators - RTGs), Propulsion (e.g., chemical or gridded ion thrusters), Comms, Science payloads, and Avionics.
  • Real-Time Systems Gauges: The platform continuously monitors total budget allocation, wet-to-dry mass ratios, power generation vs. draw balances, Tsiolkovsky V margins, science payload values, and Deep Space Network (DSN) data rates.
  • System Flight Requirements: Automated pre-flight rule checks validate core system readiness. Mission architects receive real-time engineering advisories prompting the installation of critical protective hardware, such as Multi-Layer Insulation (MLI) Thermal Blankets and Radiation Vault Shields, to survive deep-space thermal gradients and ionizing radiation environments.

Phase 3: Launch Vehicle Integration and Liftoff

Following successful blueprint authorization, the spacecraft is integrated into a verified launch vehicle fairing (matching required payload mass fractions and booster reliability ratings).

  • Pre-Flight Readiness Checklist: Validates mass fractions (wet mass vs. payload cap), financial clearance against budget limits, and booster reliability ratings.
  • Liftoff Sequence: Upon authorization, the simulator transitions to pre-launch flight decks and exterior launch pad cameras to track the rocket clearing the tower and executing powered ascent toward the chosen target orbit.

Phase 4: Interplanetary Flight Operations & In-Flight Anomaly Management

During transit, the simulator provides both First-Person Cockpit Views and Third-Person Orbital Map Perspectives, tracking Mission Elapsed Time (MET), vehicle structural integrity, remaining propellant, and communication light delays.

  • Dynamic Space Hazards & Decision Making: Flight crews face stochastic in-flight emergencies that demand immediate engineering decisions
  • Planetary Touchdown / Orbital Insertion: Powered descent or orbital insertion concludes with verified terminal contact, telemetry lock, system shutdown, and surface landmark/flag deployment.

Post-Mission Debrief, Analytics, and Design Archive

Upon successful mission completion, the Debrief Module provides comprehensive performance scoring and engineering evaluations:

  • Mission Performance Metrics: Summarizes total science downlinked, vehicle structural integrity, operational lifetime, and financial expenditure against budget thresholds, resulting in a quantifiable overall mission rating.
  • Engineering Justification Analysis: Details why the mission succeeded by cross-examining generated V margins, power generation margins during eclipse phases, and thermal/radiation shield compliance.
  • Mission Leaderboard and Design Archive: Allows designers to benchmark multiple valid mission architectures across different destinations and budgets, saving configurations locally and reloading them back into the Blueprint Bay for iterative design optimization.
